paper_title: Failure Recovery via Belief Updates and World Modeling for Long-Horizon Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Long-horizon agents tackle tasks such as autonomous research (Yamada et al., 2025), computer use (Xie et al., 2024), and sequential decisionmaking (Yao et al., 2022). However, early mistakes can propagate through long trajectories, trapping agents in repetitive attempts or leading to premature commitments that are difficult to reverse (Wang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026). The evidence needed to identify these mistakes often emerges only after many subsequent *Equal contribution. actions. Recovering from such failures requires agents to revisit earlier assumptions in light of new evidence and use what they learn to guide subsequent exploration. Reflection allows agents to revise their behavior after failures or new evidence (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023). Recovery may involve backtracking and trying another frontier, testable hypothesis for repairing the current failure. Existing approaches often organize such alternatives as tree to support branching and backtracking (Zhu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Jin et al., 2026). Long-horizon failures, however, can arise from earlier decisions or assumptions shared across branches (Zhuang et al., 2026; Rafi et al., 2026). Although rollback and persistent memory can preserve what happened, recovery still requires deciding how new verifier-grounded evidence should change the priorities of related repair hypotheses. When frontiers share prerequisites or interact across steps, evidence from one attempt can make another direction more or less promising (Zhang et al., 2026d; Liang et al., 2026). This motivates persistent exploration state that carries evidence across rollback and uses it to reprioritize future exploration. We represent exploration as persistent relational state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Recorded outcomes and candidate relations determine which unary evidence factors update each frontiers priority (Mishra et al., 2024; Cao and Chen, 2026). This lets evidence from one attempt re-rank related alternatives, while diagnostic evidence separately controls execution eligibility. The state is preserved across rollback. Belief updates capture what has been learned, but recovery also requires deciding what to try next. Recent agentic world models (Zuo et al., 2026) use learned dynamics or outcome prediction to guide decisions (Zhou et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2026). We use an implicit world model (IWM) to evaluate repair hypotheses, estimate prospective progress, and infer frontier relations, guiding their generation, refinement, and reconsideration. These repeated assessments can then be distilled into lightweight student to reduce teacher inference cost (Yang et al., 2026). In this paper, we introduce BELIEFWEAVER, framework for long-horizon problem solving that combines persistent relational exploration state with an implicit world model (IWM). The exploration state tracks frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints, preserving evidence across rollback and using new outcomes to revise related hypotheses. The IWM evaluates repair hypotheses, estimates prospective progress, and infers relations among frontiers to guide what to explore next. Execution outcomes are then added back to the persistent state, so later decisions can build on earlier attempts. Because these assessments are used repeatedly during exploration, we distill them into lightweight 9B student through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and on-policy distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024), improving task performance while reducing teacher API costs (Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025). This makes recovery cumulative: failed attempts provide evidence for subsequent exploration rather than simply triggering another retry. Our contributions are: We introduce recovery controller that uses retained execution evidence and relations among repair hypotheses to update frontier priorities. It can reprioritize candidates beyond the latest attempt, while separate diagnostic gate controls execution eligibility. We develop an implicit world model that reasons over repair hypotheses, expected progress, and their relations, and distill this reasoning into smaller student for efficient execution. Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 points over native Terminus-2 continuation and also improves exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student gains 9.8 points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8%.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: World Models for Agentic Reasoning. World models let agents reason about possible future outcomes before acting. Prior work has explored both implicit predictive models and explicit executable ones. FLARE (Zheng et al., 2025) predicts latent future observations for robot control, while Qwen-AgentWorld (Zuo et al., 2026) models agent environment transitions for general-purpose agents. RAP (Hao et al., 2023) and WebDreamer (Gu et al., 2024) use LLMs to predict outcomes during planning, and WKM (Qiao et al., 2024) combines global task knowledge with local state. Other work builds executable models for internal simulation, including WorldCoder (Tang et al., 2024) and Executable World Models (Rodionov, 2026); PatchWorld (Bai et al., 2026), OPINE-World (Courtis et al., 2026), and Tycho (Lehmann et al., 2026) further support inspection, replay, and revision. Our work instead uses consequence predictions and verifier feedback to maintain persistent belief over unresolved frontiers and guide exploration across them. Long-horizon and Recursive Agents. Longhorizon agents face context growth, evidence loss, error propagation, and difficulty recovering from earlier decisions (Chen et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a). Recent work addresses these issues through persistent state, structured search, recursion, and recovery. Argus (Zhang et al., 2026e) uses shared evidence graph to coordinate search. HTR (Jin et al., 2026) maintains persistent tree of hypotheses, artifacts, evidence, and insights, propagating experimental findings to refine and guide later search. AgentRewind (Zhuang et al., 2026) restores earlier checkpoints while retaining memories from failed attempts. Recursive Language Models (Zhang et al., 2025) recurse over subproblems, while Recursive Agent Harnesses (Lumer et al., 2026) extend this to tool-using subagents. SciNav (Zhang and Sun, 2026) frames scientific coding as search over alternative solution branches. Our controller turns retained outcomes and frontier relations into explicit priority updates through unary evidence factors, including for candidates not executed in the latest attempt. separate diagnostic gate determines which frontiers are eligible for execution. Self-Improving and Uncertainty-Guided Agents. Recent agents increasingly learn from accumulated experience or use uncertainty to decide what to explore next. SkillRL (Xia et al., 2026) jointly evolves hierarchical skill library and agent policy, while COS-PLAY (Wu et al., 2026) discovers and refines reusable skills from interaction trajectories. Darwin Gödel Machine (Zhang et al., 2026a), Gödel Agent (Yin et al., 2025), and Hyperagents (Zhang et al., 2026b) go further by iteratively modifying the agents code, logic, or improvement process. MLEvolve (Du et al., 2026) combines cross-branch search with retrospective memory, while Uncertainty-Guided Tree Search (Mhammedi and Cohan, 2026) and Agentic Uncertainty (Zhang et al., 2026c) use epistemic uncertainty to guide exploration and reflection. Our work instead uses verifier-grounded evidence to update priorities over related frontiers, allowing the agent to revisit promising directions without changing the underlying agent.

sections.title: 3 Problem Formulation
sections.content: Long-Horizon Problem Solving as Frontier Exploration. We consider an agent operating in partially observable long-horizon environment, where decisions are conditioned on the interaction history ht. Instead of modeling individual low-level actions, we formulate exploration over time-varying set of problem-solving frontiers, Ft = {f1, . . . , fNt}. Each frontier fi is testable repair hypothesis that specifies possible failure mechanism, the evidence needed to assess it, and the checks used to evaluate the repair. At step t, the agent either explores an eligible frontier or continues execution to gather evidence that can support, refine, or introduce new frontiers. The set Ft evolves over time, while identifies the same frontier across repeated attempts. Persistent Exploration State. We maintain relational graph Gt = (Vt, Rt), where Vt is the node set and Rt is the relation edge set. The graph connects frontiers with their attempts, observations, and checkpoints, and links frontiers that share or refine failure mechanisms. For each frontier fi, we maintain belief = qi bi t(zi = 1), where zi {0, 1} indicates whether the frontier remains worth pursuing and qi is the corresponding belief distribution. We summarize the exploration state as Bt = (Gt, Et, bt), bt = (bi t)fiFt, where Et contains accumulated diagnostic observations and execution feedback. Relations in Gt determine which observations activate unary evidence factors for each frontier, allowing new evidence to update the priority of related hypotheses beyond the latest attempt. New evidence et+1 is incorporated through Bt+1 = Update(Bt, et+1). The exploration state persists across environment rollback, so evidence from earlier attempts remains available for subsequent decisions. Implicit World Modeling of Exploration. Belief updates summarize what has already been learned from exploration, while choosing how to proceed requires reasoning about unexplored directions. We model this prospective reasoning with an implicit world model (IWM), ψθ(Bt, fi) = (cid:0) ˆdi t, ˆpi t, ˆri (cid:1), which assesses candidate frontier fi under the current exploration state Bt. Here, ˆdi evaluates the hypothesis against available evidence, ˆpi estimates its potential for repair progress, and ˆri captures its relations to other frontiers. These assessments guide frontier eligibility and belief revision, connect evidence across related hypotheses, and support frontier generation, refinement, and reopening. The model is implicit because it reasons directly from the exploration context rather than learning an explicit transition model of the environment. Exploration Objective. The goal of exploration is to make sustained progress toward task completion under limited execution budget. At each step, the agent uses the accumulated evidence and frontier beliefs in Bt to maintain and prioritize plausible frontiers, while allowing earlier hypotheses to be revisited as new evidence emerges. When no frontier is ready to pursue, execution continues to gather evidence and expose new repair directions. The resulting feedback supplies new evidence et+1 for updating the exploration state. The concrete gating and ranking rules are introduced in the next section.

sections.title: 4 Methodology
sections.content: We propose BELIEFWEAVER, framework for long-horizon problem solving that organizes exploration around testable repair hypotheses and evidence-grounded beliefs over which directions remain worth pursuing (Figure 1). An Implicit Figure 1: Overview of BELIEFWEAVER. BELIEFWEAVER combines evidence from past attempts with prospective reasoning over candidate repairs. Given the task and current context (Blue Box), the implicit world model (Yellow Box) proposes repair hypotheses, gathers diagnostic evidence, and estimates their outcomes. The persistent exploration graph (Gray Dashed Box) retains hypotheses, attempts, observations, and relations across rollback. Belief-guided selection (Purple Box) uses this evidence to update frontier priorities, while diagnostic evidence determines execution eligibility. The agent harness and verifier (Pink Box) execute the selected frontier and feed the outcome back into the graph. World Model proposes and evaluates candidate frontiers using targeted diagnostics and estimates of repair progress, while Persistent Global Belief State tracks their evidence and relations across attempts and rollback. Diagnostic evidence determines which frontiers are eligible for execution, and belief scores rank the remaining candidates. Execution outcomes are then added back to the state, allowing failed attempts to reshape related hypotheses and reconsider previously deprioritized alternatives. To reduce repeated teacher inference, we distill four recurring IWM roles into 9B student while keeping the recovery controller and executor unchanged. 4.

sections.title: Implicit World Model
sections.content: The implicit world model (IWM) represents unresolved failures as structured hypotheses over possible mechanisms and repairs. For each hypothesis, it asks three questions: what may be causing the failure, whether the available evidence supports that explanation, and what progress is expected from pursuing the repair. Candidate Hypothesis Generation. For each unresolved failure, language model receives the task requirements, line-indexed source context, current diagnostics, and previous attempts, and proposes testable repair hypothesis. Each proposal describes mismatch between the implementation and specification, possible underlying mechanism, relevant source locations, evidence to collect, and target check. Valid proposals are added to the frontier catalog for later evaluation. Diagnostic Probing and Evidence Judgment. For each candidate, the controller generates diagnostic command and runs it in temporary copy of the current environment. An evidence judge compares the observation with the candidates predicted current behavior and returns vi {consistent, insufficient, contradicted}. The verdict determines execution eligibility, while contradictions also add refutation evidence to the belief state. Prospective Evaluation. Two prompt-based experts estimate the consequences of pursuing each hypothesis. local_code traces the relevant control and data flow to estimate mechanism validity and progress under bounded repair attempt, while contract_judge checks whether the current implementation violates the cited task requirement. Their outputs are combined into an estimate of strict progress using the mechanism selection and outcome composition in Appendix D.3. Relation queries also identify refinements and shared mechanisms among candidates, connecting unsuccessful attempts to related hypotheses. Evidence verdicts determine execution eligibility and update beliefs, while candidate relations determine which relational evidence factors apply. Prospective estimates are used for candidate regeneration and conditional reopening. Selectable frontiers are ultimately ordered by the belief score in Section 4.2. Prompt templates, thresholds, and update rules are given in Appendix A.1.

sections.title: 4.2 Persistent Global Belief State
sections.content: Long-horizon recovery often returns to earlier checkpoints after unsuccessful interventions. We maintain persistent belief state over repair hypotheses and their evidence so that outcomes from previous attempts can shape what to explore next. We represent this state as an exploration graph Gt over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Each attempt is linked to the frontier it pursues and its starting checkpoint, while frontierfrontier relations capture shared mechanisms and hypothesis refinements. The graph and its evidence persist across rollback. For each frontier fi, we introduce binary variable zi indicating whether it remains active for exploration. sections.title: 4.4 Small-Model IWM Distillation
sections.content: The IWM relies on four recurring model-assisted probe generation, evidence judgment, roles: frontier-relation inference, and task-clause assessment. These roles use structured inputs and outputs and account for much of the repeated teacher inference, so we distill them into smaller student model.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Experiment Design. We conduct two sets of experiments. First, using DeepSeek V4 Pro (Xu et al., 2026), we evaluate the contributions of structured continuation, world-model grounding, and persistent relational beliefs through controlled ablations. Second, we distill these capabilities into Qwen3.59B (Qwen Team, 2026), comparing different distillation strategies in terms of task performance and teacher inference cost. Benchmarks. We evaluate on 113 tasks from three terminal-based benchmarks: 65 from TerminalBench 2.0 (TB2), 23 from Terminal-Bench 3.0 (TB3) (Merrill et al., 2026), and 25 from LongHorizon Terminal-Bench (LHTB) (Li et al., 2026). TB2 and TB3 cover diverse terminal tasks with testbased feedback, while LHTB emphasizes longerhorizon execution and provides score-only feedback. Together, they test recovery across different task lengths and levels of diagnostic information. Full task and evaluation details are given in Appendix C. Baselines. We compare four configurations that progressively add components of BELIEFWEAVER: (1) TERMINUS-2, the native continuation baseline; (2) + STRUCTURED CONTINUATION, adding checkpointing, candidate execution, and rollback; (3) + WM GROUNDING, adding diagnostic probes, execution feedback, and candidate-specific target checks; and (4) full BELIEFWEAVER, adding persistent relational beliefs and evidence-gated execution. All configurations start from the same checkpoint with the same remaining execution budget. Distillation. We evaluate three variants using Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026). SFT is trained on teacher responses, SFT + OPD adds teacher supervision collected during student-guided exploration, and SFT + OPD + GEN also lets the student generate repair hypotheses. The student handles probe generation, evidence judgment, candidate-relation inference, and taskclause assessment in all three settings. Repair hypotheses remain teacher-generated for SFT and SFT + OPD, while SFT + OPD + GEN generates them with the student. Prospective evaluation remains teacher-based. Both SFT and OPD train LoRA adapters with response-token cross-entropy while keeping the base model frozen. Each OPD round adds new teacher-labeled examples to the SFT data and earlier OPD data. All variants use the same executor and belief-update rules. API savings are measured against the matched teacher run. Training data and hyperparameters are given in Appendix B. Evaluation protocol and metrics. For each paired comparison, methods start from the same checkpoint and receive the same remaining execution budget. We report Final as the test-pass fraction or graded reward of the final retained checkpoint (%). sections.title: 5.2 Main Results
sections.content: Improved task performance and exploration efficiency. Compared with native TERMINUS-2 continuation, BELIEFWEAVER improves Overall Final performance by 5.1 percentage points, with the largest gain on TB3 (+10.1 points). It also improves Overall Step-AUC by 2.8 points and Time-AUC by 1.6 points, achieving the strongest aggregate results among the teacher configurations. The gains in Final and Step-AUC are significant relative to the native baseline  (Table 2)  . Together, these results show that BELIEFWEAVER not only reaches better retained checkpoints, but also makes useful progress earlier during continuation. This pattern is consistent with more effective recovery rather than gains appearing only at the end of execution. Component ablations support the combined design. We use component ablations to examine the role of each stage in the full framework. STRUCTURED CONTINUATION improves Overall Final, Step-AUC, and Time-AUC over TERMINUS-2 by 2.9, 0.9, and 1.1 points, respectively. Adding WM GROUNDING alone reduces Overall Final by 1.7 points, with small declines in both AUC metrics. Adding persistent relational beliefs and evidencegated execution on top of grounding improves Overall Final by 3.9 points, along with gains of 2.4 in Step-AUC and 1.0 in Time-AUC. The best results come from using grounding together with the full recovery controller, which updates frontier priorities from retained evidence and separately gates execution with diagnostic evidence. Since these two components are introduced together, their individual effects are not isolated. Executor savings come with greater controller overhead. Table 3 compares resource usage across the four teacher configurations. We report executor steps, execution time, logged executor cost, and controller reservations per task. Compared with TERMINUS-2, BELIEFWEAVER reduces executor steps by 13.2%, execution time by 17.8%, and executor cost by 16.6%, while achieving higher Final score. The full system uses slightly more executor resources than the intermediate ablations but attains the best task performance. It also requires more controller calls, with 33.4 reservations per task compared with 9.1 or fewer for the other configurations. This motivates distilling the recurring IWM roles to reduce teacher usage. sections.title: 5.3 Distillation Results
sections.content: Distillation transfers the recurring IWM decisions, while OPD yields higher final score. We next ask whether the model-assisted IWM roles can be moved to smaller student without losing the benefits of evidence-guided recovery. SFT already improves substantially over native TERMINUS-2, suggesting that these structured decisions can be learned from teacher supervision rather than requiring the full teacher at every step. OPD then trains the student on contexts produced by its own exploration. SFT + OPD reaches 58.4% Overall Final, 9.8 points above the native baseline, with significant Final gain  (Table 2)  . Its Final point estimate is also 4.7 points above the matched teacher. This suggests that on-policy supervision can do more than reproduce teacher outputs: it can adapt the distilled IWM roles to the states the student actually encounters during recovery. Overall, the results support simple division of labor: SFT provides the structured IWM behavior, while OPD adapts it to the students exploration distribution. The recovery controller and executor remain unchanged, so the gains come from replacing and refining the recurring model-assisted decisions rather than distilling the entire agent. Student-generated hypotheses yield the largest teacher savings. We assess distillation efficiency using executor time, teacher API requests, and estimated API cost from recorded token usage at $1/$4 per million input/output tokens. Across the tasks in Table 4, both SFT and SFT + OPD cut teacher requests and API cost by about 55% relative to the matched teacher. Moving repairhypothesis generation to the student yields larger savings: SFT + OPD + GEN reduces teacher requests by 74.5% and API cost by 81.9%, lowering the average teacher cost from $0.550 to $0.100 per task. It also reaches 57.5% Final, 3.8 points above the matched teacher. Teacher token usage follows the same pattern, decreasing by 55.4%, 55.1%, and 81.1% for SFT, SFT + OPD, and SFT + OPD + GEN, respectively. Overall, distillation substantially reduces teacher inference while maintaining strong task performance, with the largest savings when hypothesis generation is also moved to the student. These savings refer to teacher API usage rather than total end-to-end inference cost.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented BELIEFWEAVER, framework for long-horizon failure recovery built around an evidence-guided recovery controller. The controller carries verifier-grounded evidence across attempts and rollback, uses relations among repair hypotheses to update frontier priorities, and separates execution eligibility from belief-based ranking. An implicit world model supports this process by generating and evaluating repair hypotheses, estimating prospective progress, and identifying relations among frontiers. Across three terminalbased benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves task performance and exploration efficiency over native continuation. Distilling the recurring controller roles into smaller student substantially reduces teacher API usage and cost while preserving strong task performance. Future work will study learned and uncertainty-aware belief updates, finer attribution among controller components, and recovery under sparse feedback or imperfect rollback.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our framework has several limitations. Errors in IWM predictions or inferred relations can mis-rank frontiers and waste exploration effort. The current belief state also models only small set of relations between repair hypotheses, which may be too limited when several failure causes interact. Finally, our experiments focus on terminal-based tasks with verifier feedback and reliable checkpoint restoration. It remains unclear how well the framework transfers to settings where feedback is sparse or rollback is noisy or unavailable.

sections.title: A Controller Details
sections.content: Table 5 summarizes the controller settings used throughout the experiments. The following subsections describe how these settings enter belief updates, frontier selection, and execution. A.1 Implicit World Model Candidate generation. The generator receives the task requirements, line-indexed source context, current diagnostics, existing candidates, and previous attempts. It returns structured repair hypotheses containing proposed mechanism, the observed and required behavior, supporting source references, evidence to collect, target check, and an optional parent candidate. The controller validates the required fields and references before adding them to the frontier catalog. Probes and evidence verdicts. For each candidate, separate model call generates diagnostic command from the hypothesis and requested evidence. The command is executed in temporary checkpoint copy, subject to the timeout and output-retention limits in Table 5. The evidence judge compares the observed output and return code against the candidates claimed current behavior: consistent indicates supporting evidence, contradicted indicates conflicting evidence, and insufficient is used when the probe does not resolve the claim. These verdicts are used by the evidence factors and execution gate described in Appendices A.2 and A.3. Prospective evaluation and relations. The local_code expert estimates mechanism validity and expected repair progress from the relevant control and data flow, while contract_judge checks the current implementation against the cited task requirement. separate relation query identifies links such as same_mechanism and supports between candidates. These signals guide candidate regeneration and frontier reopening as exploration progresses, using the thresholds in Table 5. A.2 Evidence Factors and Belief Updates Factor model. Each frontier has binary active/inactive variable with uniform prior. Applicable evidence is represented by unary odds factors, giving relλ ui tgtλ ci ctr, t attλ ri = λ ni Oi Oi 1 + Oi bi = , (3) (4) where factor values are listed in Table 5. Candidate relations determine which unary factors apply to each frontier, but do not introduce pairwise potentials between frontier variables. Given the recorded graph and evidence, we therefore compute each frontier belief independently by local normalization. These beliefs are used to rank exploration frontiers rather than as calibrated estimates of mechanism correctness or repair success. Similarly, ui = 1 when an unfailed frontier targets component previously modified by focused attempt, and ci = 1 when its retained evidence verdict is contradicted. sections.title: B Distillation Data and Training
sections.content: Distillation setup. We distill four roles into shared Qwen3.5-9B student: probe generation, evidence judgment, candidate-relation inference, and task-clause assessment. SFT and SFT + OPD retain teacher-based hypothesis generation, while SFT + OPD + Gen adds separate generation adapter trained from the SFT checkpoint alongside the OPD adapter. Prospective evaluation remains teacher-based, with belief updates, execution gating, and task execution unchanged. Final evaluation tasks are excluded from SFT and OPD data collection, hypothesis-generation training, and development-based model selection. Training configurations are summarized in Table 6. B.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning Data. We collect 859 SFT examples from 91 tasks across TB2, TB3 (Merrill et al., 2026), and LHTB (Li et al., 2026), using DeepSeek V4 Pro (Xu et al., 2026) as the teacher. The student is initialized with SFT and further trained through three rounds of on-policy distillation. SFT + OPD + Gen combines the OPD-trained controller with separate hypothesis-generation adapter initialized from SFT. Example counts reflect requestteacherresponse pairs retained after sequence-length filtering. preserves the original request context, tool schema, and structured teacher response. We use tasklevel split of 723 training and 136 development examples. SFT Warm Start. We train on the teachers structured responses with response-token cross-entropy, using the same chat template and tool-call format as at inference time. Sampling is balanced across taskrole groups, with OPD additionally upweighting teacherstudent disagreements. We train LoRA adapters with the base model frozen and discard examples beyond the context limit in Table 6. Each run uses one nominal epoch, with 5% linear warmup followed by linear decay to 0.1 the initial learning rate. We retain the checkpoint with the lowest development loss. B.2 On-Policy Distillation Collection and weighting. OPD starts from the SFT student and follows the round and task allocation in Table 6. For each task, teacher-reference and student-assisted runs start from the same initial checkpoint. The student serves the four distilled roles, while shadow teacher labels the same requests; failed student calls may fall back to the teacher. We retain valid teacher-labeled examples from student-induced contexts, teacherreference runs, and fallback calls, and deduplicate identical requesttarget pairs within each batch. Examples are upweighted when student and teacher disagree on evidence verdicts or on same_mechanism/supports relations, in addition to the taskrole balancing used for SFT. Iterative updates and evaluation. At round k, we train on the original SFT data together with the retained OPD data from rounds 1, . . . , k, starting from the latest accepted adapter. Training uses the same response-token objective as SFT, with checkpoint selection on the combined development set. After each round, we evaluate the adapter on the fixed SFT development set. We retain it if parser acceptance is at least 95% for every distilled role and its evidence-verdict agreement with the teacher is within 2 percentage points of the previous accepted adapter, where Aprev denotes the latter agreement  (Table 6)  . The retained adapter is then used for the next round of data collection. The final student is the adapter retained after the last round, and we evaluate it from fresh initial checkpoints on the full downstream benchmarks using the same controller and execution protocol. Hypothesis-generation extension. SFT + OPD + Gen combines the final OPD adapter for the four controller roles with separate hypothesisgeneration adapter initialized from SFT. The generator replaces teacher-based candidate generation, proposing testable failure mechanisms and repair directions based on task requirements, code context, and execution feedback. It is trained on teacher requesthypothesis pairs using responsetoken cross-entropy. After filtering sequences longer than 65,536 tokens, the dataset contains 609 training and 150 validation examples. Training runs for one epoch at learning rate of 105  (Table 6)  . Downstream evaluation. We evaluate the matched teacher and student configurations from the same initial checkpoints under identical execution budgets and verification procedures. All configurations share the same executor, controller logic, and belief-update rules, differing only in model-role assignments. Shadow-teacher labeling and teacher fallback are disabled during evaluation. Task coverage and metrics are detailed in Appendix C.

sections.title: C Evaluation Protocol and Metrics
sections.content: C.1 Evaluation Procedure Tasks and shared settings. We evaluate 113 tasks: 65 from TB2, 23 from TB3, and 25 from LHTB. For each task, we run the executor until its first stop or half the total execution-time budget, then initialize all continuation methods from the same checkpoint. All methods share the executor, environment, verification procedure, and remaining budget. TB2 and TB3 provide scores and failingtest names, while LHTB provides scores only. For student evaluation, we rerun the matched teacher alongside SFT, SFT + OPD, and SFT + OPD + Gen from shared checkpoints, with shadow-teacher labeling and teacher fallback disabled. To ensure task separation, we exclude all evaluation tasks from SFT and OPD data collection, hypothesisgeneration training, and development-based model selection. Execution budgets. Each task has total executor-time budget: Bi = min(Bofficial 1200 s, 720 s, , 1800) s, TB2, TB3, LHTB. For TB2, budgets range from 600 to 1,800 seconds, depending on the task. The same budgets apply to teacher and student evaluations. After the initial execution consumes ti,0 seconds, each method receives the remaining Bi ti,0 seconds. Only executor time counts toward the budget. continuation already running when the budget is exhausted may finish, while any continuation started afterward is excluded from scoring. For checkpoints with multiple tests, we compute the score as max(r, p/(p + )), where is the official reward and and are the numbers of passed and failed tests. sections.title: D Prompts and Structured Interfaces
sections.content: We present the key prompts for hypothesis generation, evidence-based control, and prospective reasoning. Each role receives relevant task clauses, source code, hypotheses, observations, and attempt history. The excerpts follow the implementation; JSON examples illustrate tool arguments rather than actual traces. Our running example uses count(n), which should return len(range(n)) but instead returns + 1. The hypothesis count_inclusive identifies the extra increment, while test_count is the failing test. D.1 Hypothesis Generation Input. Numbered task clauses and source lines, current diagnostics, existing candidates, and attempt history. Key instructions. Each mechanism must state the concrete behavior that is wrong now, the relevant symbol/data flow, and why it causes observed failure. After failure, add materially different mechanism or narrower child. Do not prescribe old/new code, patch, or claim repair is correct. Structured output. submit_frontiers returns frontiers array. Each entry specifies the defect, predicted outcome, evidence to collect, source and task references, and target check. Source anchors cover at most 20 lines in one file, and each task reference selects one atomic clause. An optional parent_id links refinement to an earlier hypothesis. {"frontiers": [{ "frontier_id": "count_inclusive", "mechanism": "count(n) adds one, so counts are too large.", "predicted_outcome": "test_count passes.", "evidence_to_collect": "Print count(2).", "source_evidence_path": "count.py", "source_evidence_line_ids": ["L1", "L2"], "claimed_actual_behavior": "Returns + 1.", "claimed_required_behavior": "Returns len( range(n)).", "task_evidence_line_ids": ["T1"], "claimed_discrepancy": "One extra integer is counted.", "target_check": "test_count", "related_paths": ["count.py"], "parent_id": null }]} D.2 Evidence Judgment Input. The hypothesis, claimed behavior, diagnostic command, output, and return code. Key instructions. Judge the hypothesis using only the diagnostic output: contradicted: the output disproves the claimed behavior; consistent: the output confirms the claimed behavior; insufficient: the output is inconclusive (e.g., failed command, timeout, or irrelevant output). Do not rely on plausibility; if the probe contradicts the claim, label it contradicted. Structured output. submit_verdicts returns verdicts array with frontier ID, verdict, and supporting reason. For probe returning 3 from count(2): {"verdicts": [{ "frontier_id": "count_inclusive", "verdict": "consistent", "reason": "count(2) printed 3, matching the claimed extra increment." }]} D.3 Prospective Evaluation and Frontier Relations Input. Prospective evaluation uses candidate packets, current source, relevant task clauses, and portfolio context. Relation inference also considers verifier observations and attempt history. Local-code instructions. Use only the candidate packet and relevant source code. Trace local control and data flow; cited source line does not by itself establish defect. Predict the outcome of one bounded repair attempt. Structured output. For each candidate, submit_consequence_factors predicts mechanism validity and four conditional probabilities: progress under valid or invalid mechanism, large progress given nonfull progress, and full resolution given progress. separate contract judge predicts violates_contract, satisfies_contract, or insufficient, along with p_mechanism_valid, supporting references, and causal trace. The judge affects only mechanism validity, while the remaining conditional probabilities come from local code. Outcome composition. Let α and β denote the probabilities of strict progress under valid and invalid mechanism, respectively; the probability of full resolution given progress; and ℓ the probability of large progress given nonfull progress. sections.title: E Qualitative Case Studies
sections.content: We examine two archived teacher traces to show how BELIEFWEAVER uses evidence to update candidate beliefs and select executor continuations. The cases include one score-improving repair and one trajectory with no score gain. Reading the traces. Figures 2 and 3 follow four stages: failure state, candidate evidence, belief and choice, and execution result. Log excerpts and extracted fields are shown separately from condensed descriptions. The displayed values are controller beliefs, and scores are retained-checkpoint testpass fractions. Evidence, decisions, and outcomes. In Figure 2, code evidence contradicts missing-check hypothesis, shifting selection toward fuel-propagation candidate. The resulting continuation raises the score while leaving several failures unresolved. In Figure 3, belief updates redirect exploration toward the server-start hypothesis, but the retained score does not improve. Local startup succeeds, while the subsequent controller probe again fails to connect. Failure analysis. The failed case highlights gap between local execution success and retainedcheckpoint performance. The mechanism probability is distinct from the exploration belief bi Consistency checks and fallback. Before selecting m, we reconcile the judges category, probability, and causal trace using fixed lexical rules. Explicit statements about current-code behavior take precedence. trace supporting satisfaction sets satisfies_contract and caps mJ at 0.2; trace supporting violation sets violates_contract and floors mJ at 0.8. Otherwise, we retain satisfaction only when mJ 0.35 and violation only when mJ 0.5. Inconsistent judgments become insufficient with mJ = 0.5 and fall back to the local-code estimate. If that estimate is unavailable, we use (mL, α, β, ℓ, ) = (0.5, 0.5, 0.1, 0.5, 0.5). valid decisive judge may replace the default mL. Relation instructions. Do not infer relations from shared files alone; prefer call/data-flow dependencies over lexical similarity. Use supports when evidence for one candidate strengthens another, requires when acting on one depends on another, conflicts for mutually exclusive claims, and same_mechanism only for shared causes. Structured output. submit_relations returns directed candidate pairs, relation types, strengths in [0, 1], and rationales.
